patterns_found.visual_evidence: The desktop sketch shows a horizontal top navigation/header bar spanning the width of the page with navigation items aligned across the top, visually separated from the content by a horizontal rule, suggesting a persistent site header.
patterns_found.behavior_notes: Header/navigation should likely remain available while scrolling, especially on a long content page. If implemented as sticky, it should preserve access to primary navigation without obscuring content.
patterns_found.ambiguities: The sketch does not explicitly show scroll state, so fixed-on-scroll behavior is inferred from the prominent persistent header treatment rather than directly depicted.

patterns_found.visual_evidence: The mobile sketch appears to condense the top area into small boxed controls/cards rather than a full horizontal nav, implying a collapsed mobile navigation pattern instead of exposing all desktop nav items inline.
patterns_found.behavior_notes: A mobile nav toggle would open and close the primary navigation panel or drawer, likely replacing the desktop horizontal nav. Active section indication should still be preserved inside the opened menu.
patterns_found.ambiguities: The mobile sketch is highly abstract and does not explicitly draw a hamburger icon; this is inferred from the desktop presence of multi-item top navigation and the lack of room for it on mobile.

patterns_found.visual_evidence: The desktop sketch includes multiple compact nav labels/items across the top bar, matching a desktop information architecture that commonly groups sections under expandable nav items; the reference layout also strongly suggests top-level items with submenus.
patterns_found.behavior_notes: Top-level navigation items may reveal submenus on click or hover/focus. Menus should open adjacent to the trigger, close on outside interaction/Escape, and expose active/current section state.
patterns_found.ambiguities: The sketch itself does not depict open submenu panels, so the exact trigger mode (hover vs click) is not visually explicit.

patterns_found.visual_evidence: Both sketches include a chart-focused page structure with compact grouped controls near the top/content area and a large primary visualization region, implying switching between alternate data views such as chart modes or sections rather than a single static graphic.
patterns_found.behavior_notes: Tabs or segmented controls would switch visible content panels such as different metrics/views while keeping one panel active at a time. On mobile this may appear as stacked or compressed controls; on desktop it may appear inline above the chart.
patterns_found.ambiguities: The sketch does not label the controls, so this could also be a button toggle rather than formal ARIA tabs; however the mutually exclusive view-switching behavior is strongly implied.

patterns_found.visual_evidence: The dominant feature in both sketches is a large chart/graph area with supporting summary lines and changing metric displays, implying dynamically updated analytical content when the user changes view, metric, or timeframe.
patterns_found.behavior_notes: When the selected metric/view changes, summary text/status and chart-associated values should update dynamically. Important status changes such as 'loading', 'no data', or current metric selection should be announced accessibly.
patterns_found.ambiguities: The sketch does not explicitly show counters or badges; the live-update inference comes from the analytics/chart nature of the page rather than a dedicated notification element.

sketch_notes: Overall JS complexity appears moderate and centered on navigation and analytics-view switching rather than heavy form workflows. The desktop sketch strongly implies a persistent top navigation system with possible dropdowns and a large interactive chart area, while the mobile sketch suggests that navigation must collapse into a compact menu and that chart/view controls need a mobile-friendly toggle or tab treatment. No clear evidence of forms, modals, accordions, or infinite loading is present; the main cross-viewport difference is navigation presentation and control density.
